passage: Hafsa, fourteen, was taller than most of her teachers, and her body had started changing well before anyone else's in Class Nine. In PE she hunched her shoulders, kept her jacket zipped in the heat and dawdled to be last onto the court. When a group of boys whispered and laughed as she ran, she walked off and sat by the water tank. Kiran Ma'am, the school counsellor, found her there. "I look so much older than everyone," Hafsa muttered. "They all stare." Kiran Ma'am sat beside her. "Bodies change on their own timetables. Some start early, some late, and all of it is normal. Your worth isn't measured by your body. And the staring and laughing is not okay. I'll speak to the PE teacher about it today." Hafsa unzipped her jacket an inch. "Can I come back to the court with you?"

qa.q: Where did Hafsa sit after walking off?
qa.a: By the water tank.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling during PE?
qa.a: She felt self-conscious and awkward, hunching and keeping her jacket zipped to hide.

qa.q: Which parts of Kiran Ma'am's response helped, and why?
qa.a: Saying that timing varies and worth is not measured by the body, and acting on the teasing that same day, so Hafsa felt reassured and protected.

qa.q: What would change if the boys understood that timing varies?
qa.a: They might see Hafsa's body as simply normal and stop whispering, and she could run without feeling watched.

grounding: Shows a teenager who matured earlier than classmates feeling awkward and teased, and reassurance that timing varies and worth is not about the body.

passage:
Dear Yamini didi,
You said I could write about anything, so here goes. Everyone in my class has shot up this year. Rohit shaves. Even Faisal's voice has dropped. I'm still the shortest, my voice still squeaks, and in the changing room I keep my back to the wall. On Friday someone called me "little boy" in front of everyone, and I pretended to laugh. At home I stared in the mirror for ages, wondering if something is wrong with me. Our school nurse said timing is different for everyone, some people just start later, and if I'm ever worried she can arrange a check with the doctor. I want to believe her. Did you ever feel behind? How do you stop measuring yourself against everyone?
Divyansh

qa.q: What was Divyansh called on Friday?
qa.a: "Little boy".

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel after being called that?
qa.a: He felt humiliated and left behind, pretending to laugh but later wondering if something was wrong with him.

qa.q: What could help Divyansh most right now?
qa.a: Trusting the nurse's reassurance that timing varies, keeping the option of a doctor's check if worried, and hearing that his worth is not measured by his height.

qa.q: How might Yamini respond to this letter?
qa.a: She would likely feel protective and reassure him that timing varies and that his value has nothing to do with his body.

grounding: Illustrates a later-developing teenager feeling teased and left behind, and reassurance that timing varies and worth is not measured by the body.

passage: Vandana, you came home in a mood because Tara called you "baby face" again. Sit. Your Sumit Mama was the shortest boy in Class 10 in Nagpur. Everyone else had moustaches and deep voices; I still sounded like a cricket commentator's parrot. They called me Chhotu and made me carry the kit bags. I stopped taking my shirt off at swimming. I thought something was wrong with me. One day our PE teacher, Mr Kulkarni, found me hiding in the store room. He didn't laugh. He said, "Bodies run on their own clocks. Mine didn't start till I was sixteen. And the team needs your brain, not your height." He made me vice-captain that year. I grew nine inches in college. But what changed my life was that sentence, not the inches. So, baby face: your clock is fine.

qa.q: What did the boys call Sumit?
qa.a: Chhotu.

qa.q: How did young Sumit feel about being the shortest?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and left out, even thinking something was wrong with him, and hid at swimming.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Sumit saw himself?
qa.a: Mr Kulkarni telling him that bodies run on their own clocks and making him vice-captain for his brain, not his height.

qa.q: How did Mr Kulkarni see the boy hiding in the store room?
qa.a: He saw a normal late developer who needed reassurance and a role that valued him, not a joke.

grounding: Shows a late-developing teen feeling teased and awkward, and reassurance that timing varies and worth is not measured by body.

passage: The swimming gala was on Saturday, the changing room had no doors since the renovation, and over one summer Noor had grown taller and more grown-up looking than any girl in Class 8. Boys in the corridor whispered and grinned when she walked past; two girls said she "looked like a college student". On Thursday Noor told Ira she would fake a stomach ache. "I'm not changing in front of everyone." Ira didn't laugh. "Then we'll change in the staff washroom. I'll ask Ma'am." The swimming teacher, Mrs Dsouza, agreed at once, said she would speak to the boys' class teacher that day, and told Noor quietly, "Everyone's body sets its own timetable. Some early, some late. None of it decides what you're worth." On Saturday Noor swam the 50 metres and came second. She was still aware of her body. But she didn't feel like hiding it.

qa.q: What distance did Noor swim at the gala?
qa.a: The 50 metres.

qa.q: Why did Noor want to fake a stomach ache?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and self-conscious after the whispers and comments about her body, and dreaded changing in front of everyone.

qa.q: What made the difference for Noor?
qa.a: Ira took her seriously and found a private place to change, and the teacher dealt with the boys and reassured her that timing varies and doesn't decide her worth.

qa.q: How does Ira see Noor's worry?
qa.a: Ira treats it as real, not silly, and looks for a practical fix.

grounding: Shows an early-developing teen feeling teased and awkward, and reassurance that timing varies and worth is not measured by the body.

passage: At Bidisha's birthday party in their Kolkata housing complex, everyone looked older than Avni. The other girls wore heels and talked about the boys from the tuition centre; Avni, still the shortest in Class 10, felt like somebody's little sister who had wandered in. When a boy asked if she was Bidisha's cousin "from primary", she laughed, then went to the bathroom and stared in the mirror. At home she asked her mother, very quietly, if something was wrong with her. Her mother sat on the bed. "Nothing's wrong. Bodies change on different timetables; I was the last in my class too. If it ever worries you, we'll ask the doctor together. And you are not your height." The next day Bidisha messaged: "Why'd you leave early? You're the only one who laughs at my jokes." Avni smiled at her phone for a long time.

qa.q: What did the boy ask Avni?
qa.a: If she was Bidisha's cousin "from primary".

qa.q: What was Avni feeling in front of the mirror?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and left out, wondering if something was wrong with her.

qa.q: What made her mother's answer reassuring?
qa.a: She said timing varies, shared her own experience, offered to ask the doctor together if it worried Avni, and separated Avni's worth from her body.

qa.q: How does Bidisha see Avni?
qa.a: Bidisha values Avni as the friend who laughs at her jokes, not by how grown-up she looks.

grounding: Shows a late-developing teen feeling awkward and left out, and a parent's reassurance that timing varies and worth is not measured by body.

passage:
'Ammi, everyone in my class looks older than me. Zoya already looks like a college student. I still look like a little kid.'
'Who said that?'
'Nobody. Everyone. At the swimming lesson the others laughed that I look ten.'
Farida put down the knife. 'Dilnaz, come here. I was the shortest in my class till I was fifteen. Then I shot up in one year.'
'Really?'
'Really. Bodies have their own clocks. Early, late, both are normal. And none of it measures what you're worth.'
'But I feel like a baby next to them.'
'I know it feels awkward. Shall I talk to your coach about the teasing?'
'No... maybe. Yes.'
Dilnaz leaned against her mother's shoulder, a little lighter.

qa.q: Where did the others laugh at Dilnaz?
qa.a: At the swimming lesson.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz feel next to classmates?
qa.a: Dilnaz feels awkward and left behind, like a baby next to them, and hurt by the laughing.

qa.q: What reassurance did Farida give?
qa.a: That bodies have their own clocks, early or late are both normal, and none of it measures worth; she also offered to talk to the coach.

qa.q: How might Farida feel hearing about the teasing?
qa.a: Farida probably feels protective and sympathetic, remembering being the shortest in her own class.

grounding: A teenager maturing later than classmates feels awkward and teased, and a parent reassures her that timing varies and worth is not measured by body.
